evidence: Cic. Rosc. Com. 28: merēre per sē nōn amplius poterant duodecim aeris
terms.comment: Of wages and pay; stīpendia merēre is to serve as a soldier. The deponent mereor is more often “deserve” (see earn, deserve).

evidence: Ter. And. 75: lānā ac tēlā vīctum quaeritāns
terms.comment: quaeritō is ante-classical (Lewis & Short); Cato says rem quaerere for making money (Agr. praef. 1).
Used absolutely in comedy of a prostitute’s trade (Ter. Haut. 640: utī quaestum faceret; Lewis & Short s.v. quaestus).

evidence: Cic. Div. 1.111 (Lewis & Short s.v. pecūnia): to accumulate property
Traupman 161: ingentem pecūniam faciunt, they make big money

phrases.english: earning her living by spinning and weaving

phrases.latin: nam illa membra merēre per sē nōn amplius poterant duodecim aeris
phrases.english: for that body on its own could not earn more than twelve asses

sources: Lewis & Short: mereo · Lewis & Short: quaerito · Lewis & Short: quaestus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 102, 162.
